doc.title: Joseph Daley interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, March 18, 2018

title: Avant-garde and free jazz labels; Sam Rivers and structure that emerges
summary: Daley rejects the labels and describes spontaneous composition with Sam Rivers.

story.theme_name: Playing with Coltrane and the avant-garde

blocks.x: I want to talk about that. You just used the word “progressive” to describe your own music, and over the years we’ve had the word free, free jazz, and avante garde. Do you object to any of those terms?

Well avante garde means, you know, new, cutting edge. But this is music that has been played since 1971 you know. So I mean it’s not new anymore. So avant garde is a term — just to put it in a box and everything. And free jazz, if you listen to Sam Rivers and other very sophisticated progressive players, they’re not playing free. There’s a lot of structure in what they’re playing. And I don’t play free. There’s a lot of structure in what I play. I play it freely, but it’s not just playing anything at any time I want to play. Like the whole concept of, you know I was talking to you about the bass and the tuba, you know, how Herb and Howard Johnson listened to each other and worked off of each other, that’s what happens in this music, this progressive music. We work off of each other. I’m not just playing anything at any time and Warren is not just playing anything at any time. It’s stuff that, you know that we’re working to build ensemble experiences. So what we’re doing is that we’re spontaneously composing the music as we play it. And that’s the thing that was interesting about Sam. Like we get on the stage, Sam Rivers, and we get on the stage and we wouldn’t talk about anything but he’ll begin to play. And at the end of the night, if you listen to everything that we played, there was form, there was structure you know. There was this, he would do this then there was maybe a transition, then we would change keys and then this and then we’d do another mood and then we’d go this. So at the end of the night when you listen to everything put together, you see the structure of what we just finished playing. So the structure and, you know, comes after.

The final structure comes after we completed composing the piece, as it would for any composer, whether they’re Beethoven or Bach or Stravinsky. I mean their structure comes after the piece is completed.
